answer.exemplar: A sequence defined recursively is one whose terms are described in terms of earlier terms rather than in terms of the index. A rule such as a(n+1) = 2a(n) - 1 does not tell you the value of any term on its own, because it starts from a(n) and produces the next one, so it only takes effect once the first term is known. That first term has to be supplied separately for exactly this reason: a rule that refers only backwards has nothing to refer to at n = 1, and any of infinitely many starting values would generate a different sequence that still obeyed the rule. Working forwards from the starting value then gives each later term in turn, and two sequences that agree on the first term agree on every term after it, since the same rule is applied at each step. This is why a recursive rule is a complete description of a sequence only when it comes with a starting value, and why checking a claimed explicit formula means substituting back into the recursive rule rather than computing a few terms by hand.

answer.exemplar: The headline accuracy of the test describes how well it separates the two groups, but a positive result has to be weighed against how many people were in each group to begin with. Take 100,000 people: 1,000 of them have the condition and 99 percent of those, that is 990, test positive, while 99,000 do not have it and 5 percent of them, that is 4,950, also test positive. There are therefore 5,940 positive results altogether, of which only 990 are genuine, and 990 over 5,940 is exactly one sixth, or about 16.7 percent. The base rate matters because the healthy group is so much larger that its false positives outnumber the true positives even when the test is good, and the false positive rate is applied to 99 times as many people as the sensitivity is. This is why a result that looks decisive in the abstract can be weak in a rare disease. A second round of testing helps, because among people who tested positive the first time the condition is now far more common, so the base rate has risen and the same test carries more information than it did before.

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives the joint probability of having the condition and testing positive as 0.99 times 0.01, which is 0.0099, and the probability of a positive result overall is 0.0099 plus 0.05 times 0.99, which is 0.0594, and the ratio is 0.0099 over 0.0594, that is one sixth or 0.1667. Both routes show the false positives swamping the true positives, because the healthy group is 99 times larger.

questions.stem: A jar holds 4 red and 6 blue marbles, and two are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both drawn are red? Report the number only.
questions.subject: PRECALCULUS

answer.exemplar: The two routes count the same event by different means, so they must agree whenever both are set up correctly, and any disagreement points at the faulty route. The sequential route conditions at each step: the first marble is red with probability 4 over 10, and once that is known 3 reds are left among 9 marbles, so the second is red with probability 3 over 9, and multiplying gives 4 over 10 times 3 over 9, which is 12 over 90, or 2 over 15. The counting route ignores the order of the draws, which suits a question that does not distinguish between two reds in either order, so it counts 4 choose 2 ways to take two reds and 10 choose 2 ways to take any two marbles, and the ratio 6 over 45 is also 2 over 15. Reducing both to 2 over 15 makes the agreement plain. The reason the two agree is that each ordered outcome is counted three times in the numerator of the sequential route and each unordered pair three times in the counting route, so the same overcount cancels. A useful side observation is that the counting route would need adjusting if order mattered, since the ordered count of two reds is 4 times 3 rather than 4 choose 2, a factor of 3.

answer.exemplar: The three possible outcomes correspond to the three ways two non-vertical lines can relate to one another, and each case is decided by comparing the two slopes and the two intercepts. When the slopes differ, the lines have different tilts, so the vertical gap between them changes steadily as x increases and closes at exactly one value of x, which is the single meeting point and therefore the unique solution of the system. When the slopes are equal but the intercepts differ, the lines have the same tilt and stay a fixed vertical distance apart for every x, so they never meet and the system has no solution, since there is no point lying on both. When both the slopes and the intercepts are equal, the two lines coincide, so every point on that single line satisfies both equations and the system has infinitely many solutions. The same three cases reappear in the algebra, because subtracting one equation from the other leaves (m1 - m2) x equal to (b2 - b1), and that one equation has one solution when both of its coefficients are nonzero, none when only the x coefficient vanishes and the right-hand side does not, and infinitely many when both vanish. Matching the two descriptions is a good check, since a slope comparison that disagrees with the algebra points to an arithmetic slip.
